claims.text: A standard W–Cu composite contains distinct, unmodified tungsten and copper phases.
A nanometer-thick, compositionally graded W–Cu alloy interlayer can be deposited between the tungsten and copper phases during fabrication.
The graded interlayer will improve bonding at W/Cu interfaces.
The graded interlayer will lower W/Cu thermal-interface resistance.
A graded W–Cu interlayer eases the mismatch in phonon and electron transport properties between tungsten and copper.
Smoothing the abrupt property change at the W/Cu interface improves phonon and electron coupling.
Improved phonon and electron coupling across W/Cu interfaces increases the composite's effective thermal conductivity.
The graded interlayer can retain the composite's bulk mechanical strength while increasing thermal conduction.
The graded interlayer can retain resistance to irradiation-induced defects while increasing thermal conduction.
Fusion-reactor-facing applications require good thermal conductivity and resistance to neutron irradiation.
The proposed benefit will hold under high-heat-flux and irradiation conditions typical of fusion-reactor joints and heat-dissipation applications.
Conventional W–Cu composites have lower effective thermal conductivity because of resistance at sharp W/Cu interfaces.
The modified composite will have measurably higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable conventional W–Cu composite.
The modified composite will show no significant loss of mechanical performance relative to the conventional W–Cu control.
The modified composite will show no significant loss of irradiation resistance relative to the conventional W–Cu control.
The benefit depends on optimizing the interlayer thickness and composition.
An overly thick interlayer or poor interlayer adhesion could negate the improvement.
The achievable conductivity improvement may be limited by the intrinsic conductivities of tungsten and copper.
